lesson.title: One Sender, Many Destinations: Building the Multicast Tree
lesson.summary: Multicast routing is the set of protocols that build efficient delivery trees so a single stream reaches every member of a group without duplicating traffic on shared links.
lesson.body:
Multicast gives a sender a way to address a group instead of a single host, but addressing a group is only half the problem. Something still has to figure out the actual paths that carry the traffic from the source to every member of that group, wherever they happen to be, and that something is multicast routing.

Ordinary routing algorithms, the kind used for unicast traffic, are not built for this job. A shortest path algorithm answers the question "what is the best path from A to B," a single source and a single destination. Multicast needs the answer to a different question: what is the best way to get from one source to a set of destinations that can join or leave at any time and are scattered across the network. That calls for a tree, not a path, and building that tree efficiently is the real work of multicast routing.

The general solution is a distribution tree rooted at or near the source, built so that a packet is replicated only at the points where the tree actually branches, never earlier. Multicast routing protocols such as PIM in its various modes construct these trees using the underlying unicast routing table as a foundation. A common technique is Reverse Path Forwarding: a router accepts a multicast packet only on the interface that its unicast routing table says is the shortest path back toward the source, and forwards it out only on the interfaces that lead toward known group members. This simple rule prevents loops and duplicate copies without needing an entirely separate multicast topology.

Group membership itself is tracked separately, typically through a protocol like IGMP that lets a host tell its local router "I want to join this group," and the multicast routing protocol grafts branches onto the tree as members appear and prunes them away as members leave, so the tree always matches the current set of interested receivers rather than being fixed in advance.

Consider a university streaming a live orientation lecture to a multicast group address, with listening students spread across three different dormitory networks. Without multicast, the source would have to send three separate unicast copies, one per dorm, and if a link on campus is shared by all three paths, that link would carry the same video three times over. With a multicast distribution tree, the source sends one copy, it travels the shared core links once, and only splits into multiple copies at the router where the paths to the three dorms actually diverge. The savings scale with the number of receivers: whether ten students or ten thousand are watching, the shared backbone links still carry the stream exactly once.
